title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: Parts and Wholes
author: Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning
summary: This weekly teaching digest from the Episcopal Academy's Center for Teaching and Learning curates three items, each with an editorial summary and a concrete 'Try this' move, plus a closing reflection. The first points teachers heading into conferences to Crystal Frommert's Edutopia piece and its emphasis on listening early and prepping for students who are merely doing fine. The second draws on Carl Hendrick and a recent Sweller paper to explain element interactivity, the idea that deep thinking requires both command of the parts and an understanding of how they connect, and suggests asking students to explain the why behind a few facts. The third describes a field experiment with nearly 2,000 high schoolers in which giving advice to younger students modestly raised grades, tying to November's Generosity theme. It ends with the story of the Little Free Libraries as a picture of taking what helps and leaving something for the next person.
points: Teachers are urged to prepare as carefully for students who are 'doing fine' as for those in trouble, and to listen early and often in a ten-minute conference.
Element interactivity is the digest's main idea: thinking deeply requires both command of the parts and a grasp of how they connect.
A practical check is to give students a few parts of a prior unit and ask them to identify the 'why' behind each, which reveals who sees the bigger picture.
In a field experiment of nearly 2,000 students, those who spent about eight minutes advising younger students earned somewhat higher grades, though the bump mostly faded.
Each item ends with a low-cost classroom move, such as writing advice notes to next year's class and actually delivering them.
quotes: Our Portrait of a Graduate asks students to ‘Think Deeply,’ but it’s impossible to think deeply about something if you don’t have command of the requisite parts. So too is it impossible to think deeply about something if you don’t see the way the parts connect.
This holds true for a vocabulary list in Spanish class, a list of dates in History, or a series of steps in an equation in Math. This is element interactivity in a nutshell.

Hendrick closes by pointing out the importance of instructional design to ensure that disparate elements get sequenced and conveyed in such a way that a coherent narrative develops into understanding.

Try this: Give students a few requisite parts from a previous lesson or unit. Then, ask them to identify the “why” behind the atoms of information you’ve given them. How many of them are able to understand the bigger picture?
it’s her emphasis on listening early and often throughout the conversation, as well as taking extra time to prep for students who are doing “fine,” that we really appreciate.

The bump was small, and it mostly faded later in the year. But for an 8-minute exercise that cost exactly nothing, it’s a good reminder of the various ways we can help our students improve in the classroom—but also in a variety of ways that aren’t easily measured.
Before your next big test or project, ask students to write a short note of advice to next year’s class about how to tackle it. Then actually deliver the notes.
Every one of them runs on the small kind of generosity this week’s WDYN keeps coming back to: take what helps you, and leave something for whoever comes next.
